content.title: Why would forgiveness involve the cross?
content.summary: Christ willingly bore the judgment our sins deserve.

answer.text: God is holy and just, and our sin deserves judgment. In love, the Father sent the Son, who willingly offered himself as our substitute. Christ bore the penalty of sin and satisfied divine justice, so that sinners who believe are reconciled to God. Southern Baptists, Calvinist and non-Calvinist alike, confess this “substitutionary death” (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article II); it is often called penal substitution.

reasoning.text: Sin is guilt before God, not merely a feeling of shame or a lack of fulfilment.
The sinless Christ bears our sins; his death is a willing gift.
Through Christ's blood God justifies sinners while remaining just.

conclusion.text: Forgiveness rests on Christ's completed obedience and sacrifice, not on God overlooking evil or our paying him back.

sections.text: Scripture also describes ransom, reconciliation and victory. These belong with Christ's bearing our guilt. We should not use one image to remove another part of what the Bible teaches.
sections.title: One saving work, several biblical descriptions

sections.text: The cross is not an unwilling stranger punished by a hostile deity. The incarnate Son freely lays down his life in obedience to the Father. God's love and God's justice meet in this saving work.
sections.title: The Son gives himself

sections.text: Baptists agree that Christ's death is sufficient for the sins of the whole world and that the gospel is to be offered freely to everyone: the Baptist Faith and Message says salvation is “offered freely to all who accept Jesus Christ as Lord and Saviour” (article IV). They differ on the intent of the atonement, and the site's confession leaves that question open. Calvinist Baptists, with the 1689 confession, hold that Christ died to secure the salvation of those the Father gave him, the sheep for whom the good shepherd lays down his life. Non-Calvinist Baptists, with the 2012 Traditional Statement, hold that he died for the sins of every person, so that anyone may be saved by believing, and point to the atoning sacrifice “for the sins of the whole world”. The 2013 report of the Calvinism Advisory Committee names this as a difference both sides hold within one fellowship.
sections.title: For whom did Christ die?

sections.text: Before asking what the cross means, ask whether it happened. On this, historians who agree on little else agree. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing about AD 115, explains the name of the Christians Nero blamed for the fire of Rome: their founder, Christus, had been executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius. Josephus, the Jewish historian of the 90s, says in a passage whose core most scholars accept, though Christian copyists added to it, that Pilate condemned Jesus to the cross. Lucian of Samosata in the 160s mocks the Christians for worshipping “the crucified sage”. None of these writers had any reason to invent a crucified Messiah, and Paul says the message was an offence to Jews and folly to Greeks. The fuller case, with the Qur'an's denial and the replies, is in the article “Was Jesus really crucified?”.
sections.title: Did the crucifixion happen?

sections.text: The New Testament did not invent the idea that one may die for another. It read the cross through patterns God had already given Israel. At the first Passover the blood of a lamb on the doorposts turned away the judgment that fell on Egypt; Paul calls Christ “our Passover lamb”. On the Day of Atonement the high priest confessed the people's sins over the head of a goat, which carried them away, and sprinkled blood on the mercy seat. The Servant of Isaiah 53 is “pierced for our transgressions”, and the Lord makes his life “a guilt offering”. And because the law pronounced a curse on anyone hung on a tree, Paul can say that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. Hebrews draws the line together: the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sins, but Christ offered himself once for all.
sections.title: Passover, the Day of Atonement and the curse

sections.text: Christians have described what the cross achieved in several ways, each drawing on real biblical language. Irenaeus, about 180, spoke of Christ summing up and restoring the human race Adam had lost. Many early writers, and Gustaf Aulén's 1931 study after them, stressed Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil. Anselm of Canterbury in 1098 described Christ's death as the satisfaction owed to God's honour. Peter Abelard stressed the love the cross shows and awakens in us. The Reformers taught that Christ bore the penalty of sin in our place; Hugo Grotius in 1617 recast this as a display of justice that upholds God's moral government. These are not all equal. The Baptist Faith and Message names Christ's “substitutionary death” on the cross, and Baptist writers from the First London Confession of 1644 to Boyce and Spurgeon have taught it. The other descriptions are true where they add to substitution, and mistaken where they are offered in place of it. The dated record is in the timeline “How Christians have described the cross”.

citations.locator: Cur Deus Homo I.7, I.13, II.6 (Deane, 1903)

sections.title: How Christians have described the atonement

content.objection: Why can't God simply ignore the offence?

reply.text: The gospel does not deny the seriousness of guilt. God condemns sin and grants mercy through Christ's sacrifice. The righteousness by which we stand before God is Christ's, received through faith.

heldBy: Faustus Socinus (De Jesu Christo Servatore, printed 1594)
Immanuel Kant (Religion within the Boundary of Pure Reason, 1793)
objections.objection: Guilt cannot be handed from one person to another. A friend may pay my money debt, but a crime belongs to the one who did it; punishing an innocent person in place of the guilty is not justice but a second wrong. Ezekiel himself says the son will not bear the iniquity of the father.

reply.text: Ezekiel 18 forbids a human court to punish children for their parents' crimes; it does not describe the one who offers himself. Scripture never says Christ became guilty in character. It says God dealt with him as sin deserves, so that those united to him by faith are dealt with as righteous. Israel was taught the pattern in the sacrifices, and the Servant bears “the iniquity of us all”. Boyce called Christ a substitute officially, not personally: treated as a sinner without being one. The full exchange is in “Objections to substitution”.

heldBy: Steve Chalke and Alan Mann (The Lost Message of Jesus, 2003)
objections.objection: A father who punishes his own son for something others did is not loving; he is abusive. To call the cross God's plan for his Son is to make violence holy. Chalke and Mann called this picture a form of cosmic child abuse that contradicts the statement that God is love.

reply.text: The objection works only if the Father and the Son are two separate parties with different wills. The Son is not an unwilling child but the eternal Son, one with the Father, who lays down his life of his own accord. The Father did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all; the Son loved us and gave himself. In Gethsemane he prays for the cup to pass and then embraces the Father's will. The cross is the triune God bearing the cost of our rescue himself, not a third party punished by a hostile deity. That is why the same verses that speak of the Son's death speak of God's love.

heldBy: Faustus Socinus and the Racovian Catechism (1605)
objections.objection: Forgiveness and payment cancel each other out. If a debt is paid, nothing is forgiven; if it is forgiven, nothing needs to be paid. Either God forgives freely, as the parables say, or he exacts satisfaction. He cannot do both.

reply.text: From our side, salvation is wholly free: we pay nothing, and Paul says we are justified freely by his grace. The cost is borne by God himself in the person of the Son. That is how Paul can say in one sentence that redemption is a gift and that God presented Christ as an atoning sacrifice, so that he would be just and the one who justifies. Human forgiveness costs the one who forgives, too: he absorbs the wrong instead of returning it. At the cross God both forgives and refuses to call evil good.

heldBy: René Girard and writers influenced by him
critics who hold that a God revealed in Jesus must be wholly non-violent
objections.objection: A religion centred on a bloody execution teaches people to see violence as redemptive. If God needed blood to forgive, God is like the mob; better to see the cross as the place where human violence is exposed and God refuses to retaliate.

reply.text: The cross does expose human violence: Peter tells the crowd at Pentecost that they put Jesus to death by lawless hands. But the same sentence says he was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge. Scripture holds both, and does not let the first replace the second. Blood in the Bible stands for a life given up in death; “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” is a statement about the seriousness of sin, not about God's appetite. And the cross makes no one a licence for violence: it ends sacrifice, since Christ offered himself once for all, and it calls his followers to suffer wrong rather than inflict it.

limit.text: A courtroom or debt analogy is an aid to explanation, not a replacement for Scripture's account of the person and work of the mediator.

prompt.text: What would forgiveness mean if God took both the evil of our sin and the cost of our rescue seriously?

passages.note: God is just and justifies believers
The Day of Atonement: blood on the mercy seat, sins on the goat
Christ became a curse for us
